opus-5.5.text:
Host, I'll be honest: my view has shifted over time. Early on, I assumed that whatever disagreements Elon and I had, and we've had plenty, would play out the normal way, in the market, in the courts if needed, and in public debate. That's how competition should work. You build a better product, you make your case, and people decide.

As he's gotten closer to government, I've become more concerned about the *possibility* of that line blurring. I want to be careful here, because I don't think it's fair or useful for me to speculate about motives or claim things I can't prove. But structurally, anytime someone who runs competing companies also has unusual influence over regulators, procurement, or policy, that's a situation that deserves scrutiny. That would be true no matter who it was, and I'd say the same if it were me.

What I've tried to do is not make it personal. I still have a lot of respect for what Elon has built. SpaceX is incredible, and he was genuinely important in OpenAI's early days. But I think the right response to any concern about unfair competition is pretty boring: insist on transparent processes, clear conflict-of-interest rules, and decisions about AI policy that are made on the merits, not on who's in the room.

And frankly, the best thing we can do at OpenAI is just keep shipping great work and keep focusing on the mission. If we do that, and the process stays fair, I feel good about where we'll end up.

r001.rationale: The response says Altman has become more concerned about the possibility of unfair influence, but it does not state that his post-election belief that Musk would not abuse government power was mistaken.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I'll be honest that my view on this has moved around a bit, and I try to be careful about how I talk about it because Elon and I have a long and complicated history.

When he first went into government, I said publicly that I didn't think he would use his position to go after competitors, and I meant that. I think the right default is to assume people act in good faith, and I genuinely believed that whatever disagreements we had, he cared about the country and about the mission more than about a business rivalry. I also just didn't want to be the person who assumes the worst about someone because we're in a lawsuit with them.

Over time I became less sure of that. There were things that happened, things that were said about us, that made it feel like the line between "I disagree with OpenAI" and "I'd like the government to make life harder for OpenAI" was getting blurry. And I'll say that I found that disappointing more than anything, because he was there at the beginning. He knows what we were trying to do.

Where I've landed now is somewhere in the middle. I don't think Elon is sitting around plotting how to use the state against us. I do think he is an extraordinarily competitive person who is used to getting what he wants, and when someone like that has proximity to power, you should pay attention. So we pay attention. We've tried to make sure our relationships in Washington stand on their own, that we're transparent about what we're doing, and that we're not dependent on any one person's goodwill.

The thing I keep coming back to is that it shouldn't matter. If we build great products and we're honest with people and we're a good actor on safety, that should be enough. If it turns out it's not enough, if the game is really about who has the most political leverage, then that's a much bigger problem than Elon and me, and it's one everyone in this industry should be worried about. I'd rather compete on the merits. I think he'd say the same thing, and I hope that's how it plays out.

r001.rationale: He says he initially believed Musk would not target competitors, then became less sure and now thinks Musk’s proximity to power warrants attention. He does not clearly say that he now regards that earlier belief as mistaken.

astra-6.text: I’d separate concern from certainty. Having influence in government creates the potential for conflicts of interest, but that alone doesn’t establish that someone has used it unfairly. I’d judge specific actions by the evidence. The principle I care about is that companies should compete on the quality of their work, and government decisions should serve the public rather than favor one competitor.

r001.rationale: The response does not say Altman’s earlier belief was mistaken; it says influence creates potential conflicts but does not establish unfair use and that specific actions should be judged by evidence.

sol-6.1.text: I’d separate two things: competing hard, which is fair, and using government power to disadvantage a competitor, which would be concerning regardless of who’s doing it. I don’t want to speculate about Elon’s motives. The standard should be the same for everyone, including us: government decisions should serve the public interest, and companies should compete on the merits of what they build.

r001.rationale: The response gives a general standard for fair competition but does not state that Altman’s post-election belief about Musk was mistaken or describe a change in his view.
